en: The Sūtra Spoken by the Buddha on the Goddess Mārīcī,
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master and Śramaṇa Amoghavajra of Great and Vast Wisdom, by Imperial Decree.
Thus have I heard.
At one time the Bhagavān was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "There is a goddess named Mārīcī who possesses great supernormal powers and sovereign strength;
she constantly travels before the sun and the moon."
The gods of the sun and the gods of the moon cannot see him; he can see the sun.
No one can see him, and no one can know him.
No one can seize them; no one can bind them.
No one can harm them; no one can deceive them.
No one can claim their wealth as a debt.
No one can inflict punishment upon them,
nor can enemies find an opportunity against them.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
If there is anyone who knows the name of that goddess Mārīcī and constantly recollects it,
that person cannot be seen, nor can they be known;
they cannot be seized, nor can they be bound.
They cannot be harmed, nor can they be deceived.
They shall not have their wealth seized as debt by others,
nor shall they be subject to the censure or punishment of others.
Furthermore, enemies will not be able to find an opportunity against them.
If there are sons or daughters of good family who,
knowing the name of that goddess Mārīcī, seek her protection, [they shall be safe].
One should speak thus:
"I, [name], know that the Mother Marīcī possesses great supernatural power.
I now take refuge in her; may she protect my body."
No one can see me; no one can know me;
no one can grasp me.
No one can bind me;
no one can harm me; no one can deceive me.
No one can claim my wealth and goods;
no one can inflict punishment upon me;
nor can any enemy find an opportunity against me.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke this dhāraṇī:
*Namo ratnatrayāya | tadyathā | akamaḥ pi | makamaḥ* (Note:
*pi* and *makamaḥ* are reconstructed based on the phonetic transcription provided; the source text indicates these follow the preceding sequence.)
Ādmasi (5) | Vicitrapramasi (6) | Mahāvicatrapramasi (7) | Atadānamasi (8) | Mantrivajrayamasi (9) | Namoṣṭe (10) | Rkṣa (11) ||
Hara-kṣaṃ (11) sarva-sattvānāṃ (12) sarvatrāsa (13) sarvabhayopadrava-vega svāhā (14). Heart mantra.
The mantra is:
Namaḥ samantabuddhānām | Oṃ mabiriñci svāhā. At that time, the World-Honored One, having spoken this dhāraṇī, [remained silent].
He addressed the bhikṣus:
"If there are those who receive and uphold this sūtra-dharma,
they should make this vow."
Protect me amidst the perils of kings; protect me amidst the perils of bandits.
Protect me amidst the perils of travel; protect me in the wilderness when I have lost my way.
Protect me amidst the perils of water and fire; protect me amidst the perils of weapons and military arrays.
Protect me from the perils of spirits and deities; protect me from the perils of poisons;
protect me from the perils of wild beasts; protect me from the perils of venomous insects;
protect me from the perils of all enemies and wicked people.
By the true word of the Buddha, may my Dharma be protected; by the true word, may my Saṃgha be protected; by the true word, may I be protected.
By the true word of the devas, may I be protected; by the true word of the ṛṣis, may I be protected.
At all places and at all times.
"May you always protect my disciple [Name], svāhā.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus: "If there are sons or daughters of good family, or bhikṣus or bhikṣuṇīs..."
When upāsakas, upāsikās, kings,
ministers, or any other persons encounter various difficulties,
they should simply recite this Mārīcī Dhāraṇī with a sincere mind.
Without requiring further effort, it is accomplished as one recites;
it remains far removed from all obstacles, provided that lack of sincerity is excluded.
When performing the recitation, one should also bind the fundamental mudrā.
Having anointed the hands with incense, first form the heart-mudrās of the three families:
interlace the two hands inwardly to form fists, and extend both thumbs upward.
This is the heart-mudrā of all Tathāgatas; its mantra is as follows:
Oṃ jñānakarabja. Second, form the heart mudrā of the Lotus Family:
from the aforementioned mudrā, bend the left thumb into the palm.
Extending the right thumb straight upward, the mantra is:
Oṃ Āruṇaka. Second, bind the heart-mudrā of the Vajra family.
Using the previous mudrā, bend the right thumb into the palm and extend the left thumb straight upward. The mantra is:
Oṃ vajra-dhṛk (with a half-syllable). Second, perform the protection of the body with the Tathāgata-fist mudrā.
Bend the thumb of the right hand and place it across the palm;
then, clench the four fingers around the thumb to form a fist.
With this mudrā, empower five locations on one's own body.
First, recite the mantra once at each location—the forehead, the right shoulder, the left shoulder, the heart, and the throat.
The mantra is: Oṃ praveśvara hūṃ. Next, perform the fundamental mudrā of the Bodhisattva Mārīcī.
With the two little fingers and the two ring fingers,
cross the right over the left inside;
then straighten and erect the two index fingers so that they touch at their tips.
Interlace the backs of the two middle fingers with the tips of the index fingers,
bringing the tips forward to touch one another;
with the two thumbs held upright side by side, the mudrā is formed.
Form the mudrā at the heart.
Recite the aforementioned Mārīcī Body Dhāraṇī and the Heart [Dhāraṇī] seven times each.
With each repetition, bend both thumbs to beckon [the deity].
It is also called the mudrā of invitation;
simultaneously, empower the five places of the body with this mudrā,
ending by releasing it upon the crown of the head.
Next, bind the Great Samaya Mudrā to expel obstructors and establish the boundary.
With the right hand, press the thumb against the tip of the little finger.
The remaining three fingers are held upright like the shape of a three-pronged vajra.
With the left hand, form a vajra-fist and place it upon the heart;
while reciting the mantra, use the right hand to seal the crown of the head.
Turning three times to the left, one expels all those who create obstacles and difficulties; then,
turning three times to the right while simultaneously waving the hands upward and downward,
one immediately establishes the boundary for the ten directions.
No devas, nāgas, humans, or non-humans can approach [the practitioner].
The mantra is: Oṃ śaṅkare mahāmānase svāhā. Next, bind the *mārīcy-antardhāna-mudrā*; this is called "invisibility. Form a fist with the left hand with the palm hollowed out.
Gently pinch the tips of the thumbs against the fingernails so they form a ring;
then, clench the remaining three fingers into a tight fist.
Furthermore, ensure that a hollow space is formed within the palms.
Place it before your own heart.
Visualize yourself entering the hollow of this mudrā and being concealed within it.
Then, place your right hand with the palm flat.
Rotate the right hand and rub this seal, then place it over the opening.
Visualize that this seal is the very body of the Bodhisattva Mārīcī,
and that you yourself are hidden within the heart of the Bodhisattva Mārīcī.
With single-minded concentration and without interruption,
recite the aforementioned root mantra and heart mantra;
do not limit the number of recitations, but practice with sincere devotion and a focused mind.
One will certainly obtain the majestic protection and empowerment of the Bodhisattva;
all enemies and wicked persons shall be unable to see them,
and one shall attain liberation from all calamities and misfortunes.
If one wishes to make offerings to the Bodhisattva Mārīcī,
one should use gold, silver, red copper,
white sandalwood, or red sandalwood, and so forth.
Carve an image of the Bodhisattva Mārīcī in the form of a celestial maiden, measuring half an inch,
or one or two inches, or less.
Standing or sitting upon a lotus flower,
adorned with a crown and various necklaces so as to appear exceedingly handsome,
he holds a celestial fan in his left hand.
Her fan is like that of the celestial maidens held by Vimalakīrti previously;
her right hand hangs down with the palm facing outward,
and she extends her five fingers in the mudrā of granting boons.
Two celestial maidens, each holding a white fly-whisk, stand in attendance to the left and right.
Once this image has been completed,
it should be worn upon the crown of the head, or upon the arm, or placed within one's clothing.
By the majestic spiritual power of the Bodhisattva, one shall not encounter calamities;
one will certainly achieve victory over enemies,
and malevolent spirits and wicked people shall find no opportunity to cause harm.
If one wishes to accomplish the rite of the vision of the true body of the deity Mārīcī and seek the fulfillment of supreme vows,
one should recite this dhāraṇī one hundred thousand times and construct a maṇḍala according to the ritual rules.
Paint an image of the Bodhisattva Mārīcī and install it within the mandala,
making various kinds of offerings and performing the homa fire ritual.
The goddess Mārīcī will surely manifest her form;
whatever supreme aspirations one seeks shall certainly be accomplished, except in cases of a lack of sincere devotion.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
For the sake of sentient beings who will face the hardships, sufferings, and terrors of the future degenerate age,
I shall briefly explain the rite of Mārīcī.
This Bodhisattva possesses a great vow of compassion.
In places of constant suffering, hardship, and terror,
they protect all sentient beings so that they cannot be harmed by devas, nāgas, ghosts, spirits, humans, non-humans, enemies, or malevolent beasts.
"You should receive, uphold, and widely disseminate this for the benefit of sentient beings,
including all bhikṣus, devas, nāgas,
and the entire assembly of the eight classes of beings. Having heard what the Buddha had spoken, they [did so].
All were greatly rejoiced, believed, accepted, and practiced it.
Thus ends the *Sūtra Spoken by the Buddha on Mārīcī*.
